deed: החובש ברנרד בר-נתן החליף תחבושת שלא השתנתה מאז מלחמת העולם השנייה
title: Medic Bernard Bar-Natan replaced the World War II bandage, and it entered the world's armies

trailer.text: Bernard Bar-Natan, an American-Israeli and a former combat medic in the IDF, is the inventor of the emergency bandage known as the Israeli Bandage.
Bernard Bar-Natan, a Jew from Brooklyn and the son of Holocaust survivors, immigrated to Israel in 1979 and was a medic in the Israeli army.
In the IDF Medical Corps he discovered that the army's bandages had been made around the time of World War II and had not been changed since.
He invented a bandage with a built-in handlebar that replaces the stone medics placed on the wound, and it can apply up to about 30 pounds of pressure.
According to the Jerusalem Post, the bandage is manufactured at the factory of Ahmad Heib, a Bedouin Israeli factory owner who employs women.
Today the bandage is standard issue for the IDF and the armies of the United States and Britain, and it is also used by emergency responders and hospitals around the world.

paragraphs.text: Bernard Bar-Natan immigrated to Israel from Brooklyn in 1979.
In the 1980s, a few years after immigrating, he began thinking about bandages.
When he joined the IDF Medical Corps, he was shocked to learn that the army's standard bandages had been made around the time of World War II and had not been changed since.
He was annoyed that the manufacture date could be 1942 or the previous month, and yet the bandages had barely changed.
Bar-Natan told JTA that the weapons and the planes had improved, but the bandages had stayed the same.
Bar-Natan was taught to take a stone and add bandages over the wound to stop the flow of blood.
Ofer Molad says that he and his fellow soldiers in the IDF also used to wrap a rock in the bandage to maintain the right pressure.
Medics in the field had to improvise pressure applicators from whatever was at hand: magazines, rocks and canteens.
According to the Jerusalem Post, these methods were unsanitary, and medics had to carry many bandages.
In the past, medics and soldiers needed three or four different dressings to bandage a wound.
According to Israel21c, even in the Gulf War in the early 1990s, American soldiers sometimes used bandages from the World War II period.
JTA: He was drafted into the army in 1983

stations.title: A handlebar instead of a stone

paragraphs.text: Bar-Natan invented a bandage with a built-in handlebar, which took the place of the stone.
The handlebar can apply up to about 30 pounds of pressure to stop bleeding, even in traumatic head injuries.
He also invented a "reverse wrap" technique: you wrap around the wound, change direction and wrap the limb, and so the pressure increases without additional bandages.
One bandage with the elastic cloth is enough for a head wound, because the wrapping around the head itself applies pressure.
It can be put on with one hand, as Ofer Molad demonstrates.
One of the models covers both an entry wound and an exit wound.
By the early 1990s, Bar-Natan already had a prototype of the bandage.
According to JTA, it was invented in 1993.
In the early 1990s the Israeli government encouraged startups with low-interest loans, and this encouraged Bar-Natan.
With the help of a government grant and an Israeli accelerator program he launched the business, but he had no way to manufacture the bandage in large quantities.
His company, First Care Products, was a small four-person Jerusalem startup.
The total investment in the company reached $900,000, of which $300,000 was invested initially by the Office of the Chief Scientist.
In 1997 Ofer Molad came to the Jerusalem incubator to look for software technologies, and found the bandage there.
Bar-Natan was looking for a manufacturer for the bandage, and Ahmad Heib had a factory.
An acquaintance from the garment industry introduced them, thinking the two could help each other.
Bar-Natan was a cosmopolitan Jew from Brooklyn, and Heib was a Muslim who grew up in a remote rural corner, notorious for crime and gangs.
At first Heib worked with Bar-Natan from a small factory on the first floor of his house in Tuba-Zanghariya, a town of about 6,000 residents.
As they worked together, a friendship formed between them, especially after two of Heib's children died at birth.
Heib expanded the factory to three floors, which can produce millions of bandages a year.
Women work at the factory, and they manufacture the bandage.
Heib said that without the factory, these women would not be working.
Arij Kabishi, a Druze woman in charge of quality control at the factory, is grateful for the work and proud of her role.
According to the Jerusalem Post, the partnership between the Jewish medic and the Bedouin factory owner is one of the prominent examples of diversity in Israel.
The company's first break came in 2000, when Robert Miller, a medic and trainer in the 75th Ranger Regiment, showed interest in the product.
That same year Miller took the bandages to Bosnia and began using them on the battlefield.
Also in 2000, Bar-Natan brought the bandage to Fort Sam Houston in San Antonio, where the US military trains medics.
Bar-Natan's company, First Care, sold the bandage to elite units, including the 75th Rangers and the 101st Airborne.
American soldiers called it the Israeli Bandage.
According to the Jerusalem Post, the Australian military, the New Zealand military and most NATO countries have adopted the bandage.
It is standard issue for the IDF and the armies of the United States and Britain.

According to a January 2005 article, First Care was then also selling the bandages to military and government organizations worldwide, including the Canadian forces, the French Army and the Belgian Army.
Emergency responders and hospitals around the world also use the bandage.
According to Israel21c, the US Army purchased nearly 200,000 bandages in one year, and 800,000 the following year.
According to a January 2005 article, about 90 percent of First Care's sales were then to the US, and 10 percent to the rest of the world.
The company expected to close 2004 with sales of about $2.5 to 3 million, and according to the forecast this was to be its first profitable year.
According to Israel21c, this is the first major change to field dressings since the 1940s.
On January 8 there was a shooting in Tucson, in which six were killed and 13 wounded.
According to JTA, the victims were saved in part thanks to an Israeli bandage invented by an immigrant from Brooklyn during his service in the Israeli army.
First responders credited "the Israeli bandage" with saving lives after the shooting.
David Kleinman, a SWAT team medic who devised a first aid kit, said that in the Tucson shooting the sheriffs reached for the bandage again and again.
Dr. Katherine Hiller, who treated the wounded, told the Los Angeles Times that without this care the situation would have been completely different.
Pima County officials displayed the kit at a news conference in Tucson on January 21.
It is not clear whether the bandage was applied to Gabrielle Giffords, because the details of the day were lost in the chaos.

Israel's ambassador in Washington, Michael Oren, told the conservative website Daily Caller that the moment he learned of the bandage's role in saving lives in Tucson was one of the highlights of his term as ambassador.
The company was told that the US Army buys new products only once every four years, and that it had just completed such a process.
In the civilian market the company could not compete, because the bandage is more expensive than most existing options.
